patients.summary: Young man with bilateral cataract surgery at 20 who joins in 2020, is diagnosed with myotonic dystrophy type 1 by neurology in 2023, Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) with azoospermia by genetics in 2024, and AV conduction disease by cardiology in 2025. By 2026 he has dysphagia, weight loss and confirmed low testosterone, and is weighing fertility options before any testosterone.

documents.title: New Patient Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
22 y/o M here to establish. Last regular care was his pediatric practice in high school. Feels well. No complaints today.

PMH: none ongoing. Cataracts in both eyes found at 20; had them taken out with lens implants, right then left, summer 2018 at an outside surgery center. Vision fine with glasses for reading now and then. Says he had some trouble with reading in school, thinks it was mild dyslexia, never formally treated.
PSH: bilateral cataract extraction w/ IOL (2018).
Meds: none. No supplements.
Allergies: NKDA.
FHx: father has a muscle disease, pt not sure what it is called, and also had cataracts young. Mother healthy. Nothing known on mom's side.
SHx: works part time on the sales floor at a store in town. Lives on his own, has a girlfriend. Never smoked, does not drink, no drugs. Right-handed.

ROS: negative in full except as above.

Exam: tall, thin young man, NAD. HEENT: pupils round and reactive, IOLs in place, TMs clear, oropharynx clear. Neck supple, no thyroid enlargement. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender. Skin without rash. Strength and gait grossly normal.

A/P
1. Health maintenance: screening HIV and hep C, CBC, CMP, lipids. Flu vaccine given. PHQ-2 negative. Will get childhood shot records and Tdap date from old office.
2. History of bilateral cataract surgery at 20, pseudophakic. Eye follow-up with his surgeon as they advise.
3. Family history of a muscle disease in father: asked him to find out the name from his dad.
RTC 1 year.

documents.title: Your lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Zachary, all of your blood work from Tuesday is normal: blood counts, kidney and liver tests, cholesterol, and the HIV and hepatitis C screens were both negative. Nothing to do. Good to meet you.

documents.title: Prior pediatric office and eye surgery records
documents.author: MA
documents.body:
Received by fax, 31 pages.

Pediatric office (care through 2016): routine well visits, normal growth with a fast height gain in the teen years. Childhood immunization series complete. Tdap 08/11/2015. No chronic conditions listed.

Outside eye surgery center: bilateral visually significant cataracts in a 20 y/o. Right eye phacoemulsification with posterior chamber IOL 07/10/2018, left eye 08/07/2018. Both uncomplicated. Post-op visits with good acuity in each eye.

Abstracted into chart. Scanned to media. Routed to PCP.

events.reason: Hand stiffness, can't let go of grip

orders.reason: grip myotonia, weakness, family history of muscle disease

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Several months of his hands "sticking." Started golfing with coworkers this spring and after a swing he can't open his hand off the club right away. Same thing shaking hands with customers and with doorknobs. Takes a few seconds to let go. Also more tired than usual and feels his hands and lower legs are weaker. Over the last few weeks a little harder to get up from a low chair, feels clumsy walking on uneven ground. No numbness, no pain, no rash.
Family: dad's muscle disease started in his early 30s and pt says this sounds like what dad describes.

O: Thin, well. After a tight fist he is slow to open his fingers, improves with repeating it. Strength grossly 5-/5 in hand grip and ankle dorsiflexion, otherwise 5/5. Reflexes symmetric. Gait normal on flat floor. Heart regular.

A/P: Grip release delay with mild distal weakness and a father with a similar muscle disease. Concerned for an inherited myotonic disorder. CK today. Referral to neurology, asked them to see him this summer. Pt agrees.

documents.title: CK result
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Zachary, your CK (a muscle enzyme) came back at 284, a bit above the normal range. That fits with what we talked about and I've sent it along with the referral. Neurology should call you to schedule; let me know if you haven't heard from them in two weeks.

documents.title: Neurology visit
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Saw neurology last Monday. She said it is probably myotonic dystrophy, the same thing my dad has, and they sent a genetic test. Did you get her notes? She said my legs are a little weak at the ankles too.

documents.title: RE: Neurology visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Thanks for letting me know. We have not received the note yet. I'm asking our staff to request it today, along with the genetic test result when it is back. Let's meet once I have it.

documents.title: Records request
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Called the neurology office, spoke with their records clerk. Requested 8/14 consult note and pending genetic testing. Faxed our request form and signed release. They said 1-2 weeks.

documents.title: Records request, second attempt
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Neurology note from 8/14 still not here. Called their office again; clerk says the note was waiting on the genetic result to be added. Will send both once signed. Re-faxed release.

documents.title: Neurology consultation (visit 08/14/2023)
documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
NEUROMUSCULAR CLINIC: CONSULTATION
Date of service: 08/14/2023
Referred by: primary care, for difficulty releasing grip

History: 25-year-old right-handed man. The problem first showed itself on the golf course: after swinging he could not unclench from the club. He has the same trouble disengaging from a handshake and from doorknobs. For several months he has felt more fatigued, with mild weakness he localizes to the hands and the lower legs. More recently he struggles to stand from a chair and feels unsteady on uneven ground. His father developed a muscle disorder in his early thirties with complaints much like these.

PMH: bilateral cataracts removed at 20 with lens implants. No medications. NKDA. Never smoker, no alcohol. Part-time retail sales associate.

Examination: Grip myotonia, with delayed relaxation after sustained handgrip. Mild foot drop on both sides. Receding hairline with early frontal balding. No skin rash and no joint deformity. Remainder of the neurologic examination without focal deficit.

Data: Creatine kinase from his primary care office 284 U/L, mildly elevated.

Impression: Grip myotonia with distal-predominant weakness, early frontal balding, cataracts at a young age and an affected father. Clinical picture is myotonic dystrophy type 1.

Plan: DMPK repeat analysis sent. Discussed autosomal dominant inheritance. Follow up in the neuromuscular clinic.

ADDENDUM 09/08/2023: DMPK testing shows an expanded CTG repeat on one allele, estimated at about 420 repeats. This confirms myotonic dystrophy type 1. Result reviewed with the patient by phone.

Allergies: NKDA. Copy to primary care.

documents.title: Neurology letter reviewed
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Neuro consult and DMPK addendum reviewed. DM1 confirmed, ~420 CTG repeats. Added to problem list. Pt already has a follow-up with me 10/10.

orders.reason: myotonic dystrophy type 1, family planning, 5 months trying to conceive

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
F/u after neurology. DM1 confirmed by gene test (~420 repeats). He took it in stride; his father has the same diagnosis and pt has watched it for years. Hands about the same. Still working.

New question: he and his girlfriend have been trying for a baby since around May without a pregnancy. Wants to know if his diagnosis changes anything for having kids.

No meds. NKDA.
Exam: hand grip release slow, unchanged. Mild bilateral ankle dorsiflexion weakness. Heart regular. Lungs clear.

A/P
1. Myotonic dystrophy type 1. Neuromuscular clinic following. Basic labs today (CMP, A1c, TSH) for a baseline.
2. Trying to conceive, ~5 months. Discussed that DM1 can pass to a child and that genetics can go over family planning options with both of them. Referral to medical genetics. Semen analysis ordered as a first step; instructions given (2-5 days abstinence, sample to lab within an hour).
3. Flu shot today.
RTC after genetics.

results.text: Absent. No spermatozoa of any kind seen, including on examination of the centrifuged pellet.

documents.title: Semen analysis result
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Zachary, the lab did not find any sperm in the sample, including when they spun it down to look more carefully. This is called azoospermia. It has several possible causes, and it is exactly the kind of thing the genetics team should look at. I've sent the result to them ahead of your February appointment. Happy to talk by phone before then if you want.

documents.title: RE: Semen analysis result
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Ok. Kind of a lot to take in. We'll wait for the genetics appt. Thanks for sending it over.

documents.title: Medical genetics consultation (visit 02/06/2024)
documents.author: medical genetics
documents.body:
MEDICAL GENETICS CONSULTATION
Date of visit: 02/06/2024
Reason: myotonic dystrophy type 1; infertility

History: 25-year-old man seen roughly six months after his neuromuscular diagnosis of DM1 (DMPK expansion, about 420 CTG repeats). He and his partner have been trying for a pregnancy for about nine months. He has never fathered a pregnancy. He describes erections and libido as normal. Recent semen analysis from his primary care office showed azoospermia. His parents remember a growth spurt in adolescence; he has always been tall and lean, which the family put down to genetics. Right-handed. Had trouble learning to read and calls it mild dyslexia. Otherwise healthy apart from cataract surgery in both eyes at 20. Takes no medications. NKDA.

Family history: father with DM1 and early cataracts; paternal grandfather with weakness and grip myotonia, never diagnosed; mother healthy; no known genetic conditions on the maternal side.

Social: works part-time in retail and lives on his own. Did not play team sports growing up and remembers feeling somewhat awkward next to classmates.

Examination: Height 6 ft 2 in, with legs long in proportion to the trunk. Pleasant and cooperative, a little reserved. Little facial or chest hair, sparse axillary hair. Gynecomastia present. Testes palpable on both sides, small and firm. Neurologic examination normal.

Studies: Scrotal ultrasound, no structural abnormality of either testis or of the vasa deferentia. Buccal smear: a dense, darkly staining chromatin body at the nuclear margin in many somatic cells, consistent with an extra X chromosome. Testicular biopsy not performed.

Assessment:
1. Klinefelter syndrome, suspected on exam and buccal smear; peripheral blood karyotype sent for confirmation.
2. Male infertility with azoospermia, explained by #1.
3. Myotonic dystrophy type 1: counseled that each child of his would have a 50% chance of inheriting the expansion, with possible lengthening of the repeat when passed on.

Plan: karyotype; fertility options to be discussed further if the couple wishes to pursue them; return as needed.

Copy to primary care.

documents.title: Genetics letter reviewed
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Genetics letter reviewed. Klinefelter suspected on exam and buccal smear, karyotype pending. Azoospermia attributed. Added Klinefelter and male infertility to problems; family hx updated (father DM1, early cataracts; PGF undiagnosed weakness/myotonia). F/u with pt 3/12.

documents.title: Genetics addendum: karyotype
documents.author: medical genetics
documents.body:
ADDENDUM to consultation of 02/06/2024
Peripheral blood chromosome analysis: 47,XXY in all 20 cells counted. Confirms Klinefelter syndrome. Discussed with the patient by telephone 03/01/2024.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, low MDM

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Here to go over genetics. Karyotype 47,XXY, so Klinefelter, and that explains the azoospermia. He says it was strange to learn this at 25 but a lot of things about growing up make more sense now. He and his partner are taking a break from trying for now and may go back to genetics about options later. Mood ok, sleeping fine, working.

Hands unchanged. No new weakness.
Exam: BP and HR fine. Wt 78. Grip release slow. Heart regular.

A/P
1. Klinefelter syndrome, 47,XXY. Male infertility, azoospermia.
2. Myotonic dystrophy type 1, neuromuscular clinic following.
Physical in the fall.

events.reason: Fatigue, short of breath jogging, skipped beats

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

orders.reason: myotonic dystrophy type 1 with exertional fatigue and sensation of irregular heartbeat

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Started jogging in the fall to get in shape and finds he gets winded fast, sooner than he thinks he should. More tired in general. Some nights lying flat in bed he feels like his heart pauses or skips. No chest pain, no lightheadedness, has never passed out. Not short of breath at rest or walking around the store.

O: BP and HR normal, SpO2 normal. Wt 77.5. Heart rate regular during exam, no murmur. Lungs clear. No leg swelling.

A/P: DM1 with exercise intolerance and a sense of irregular beats lying down. Heart involvement is a known part of DM1 and he has never had a cardiology evaluation. Referral to cardiology, asked for a prompt visit; their office does the ECG and any monitoring. Baseline ECG 2022 normal, sent with the referral. Call or go to the ED for fainting, chest pain, or near-fainting.

documents.title: Cardiology
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Saw the heart doctor last week. They said my ECG showed a slow electrical signal and I'm wearing a monitor for 2 days starting the 11th. Echo was normal. Just letting you know.

documents.title: RE: Cardiology
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Thanks, Zachary. Glad the echo was normal. I'll watch for their note and the monitor results. Call if you feel faint at any point.

reports.text: PA and lateral views. Cardiac silhouette is normal in size. No pulmonary edema or vascular congestion. Lungs clear. No pleural effusion. Bones unremarkable.

Normal left ventricular size and wall thickness. Normal left ventricular systolic function with no regional wall motion abnormality. Right ventricle normal in size and function. Valves structurally normal without significant regurgitation or stenosis. No pericardial effusion.
reports.conclusion: Normal left ventricular function. No valvular disease.

reports.text: Sinus rhythm, rate 66, regular. PR 236 ms. QRS 94 ms with normal morphology. No dropped beats. Compared with tracing of 02/08/2022 (PR 168 ms), PR prolongation is new.
reports.conclusion: Sinus rhythm with first-degree AV block, new since 2022.

documents.title: Cardiology consultation (visit 01/29/2025)
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
CARDIOLOGY CONSULTATION
Visit date: 01/29/2025
Referred by primary care: DM1 with fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance

HPI: 26-year-old man with myotonic dystrophy type 1 and Klinefelter syndrome. Gets out of breath quickly when he jogs. At times, mainly when lying flat, he senses a beat that comes late or out of rhythm. He denies chest pain, palpitations as such, dizziness and syncope. Sleep is normal. Drinks little caffeine and no alcohol.

Meds: none. Allergies: NKDA.
Family history: father with DM1 and premature cataracts; paternal grandfather with undiagnosed weakness and grip myotonia; mother healthy.

Exam: Blood pressure and heart rate normal. Apical pulse slightly irregular. No murmurs, rubs or gallops. Lungs clear. No edema.

Studies today:
- Chest x-ray: normal heart size, no edema or vascular congestion.
- Echocardiogram: normal LV function, valves normal.
- ECG: regular sinus rhythm with PR 236 ms, normal QRS, no non-conducted P waves. Prior ECG from three years ago had a normal PR, so this is new.

Assessment: First-degree AV block, new, in a young man with DM1. Conduction system involvement is expected in this disease and needs surveillance. Structural heart is normal.

Plan: 48-hour ambulatory ECG monitor to look for higher-grade block. Follow-up after the monitor. He knows to report fainting or near-fainting right away.

cc: primary care

documents.title: Cardiology letter reviewed
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Cards consult reviewed. CXR and echo normal. New 1st degree AVB, PR 236 (was 168 in 2022). Monitor ordered by them. Added to problem list.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, low MDM

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
F/u. Wore the heart monitor for 2 days in February and saw cardiology again in April. Per pt, they told him there were some "skipped beats" mostly while he was asleep, that he does not need a pacemaker now, and that they will repeat the ECG and monitor every year. We have not received the monitor report or the April note.

Still tires easily; has backed off the jogging and walks instead. No fainting or near-fainting.

Exam: well. Heart regular today, no murmur. Lungs clear.

A/P
1. First-degree AV block, DM1-related per cardiology. Awaiting April letter and monitor report; staff to request.
2. DM1, Klinefelter: stable.
Physical in October.

documents.title: Records request
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Faxed request to cardiology for the 2/11 ambulatory monitor report and 4/8 office note. Called to confirm receipt, left message with their records line.

documents.title: Cardiology follow-up (visit 04/08/2025)
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
CARDIOLOGY FOLLOW-UP
Visit date: 04/08/2025

Interval: Wore a 48-hour ambulatory monitor beginning 02/11/2025. No symptoms recorded in the diary other than fatigue. No syncope or presyncope.

Monitor review: Sinus rhythm with first-degree AV block throughout. Intermittent second-degree AV block, type I, predominantly during sleep. Longest pause 2.2 seconds. No higher-grade AV block. No atrial fibrillation or flutter. No ventricular tachycardia.

Exam: BP and HR normal. Rhythm mildly irregular. No murmur.

Assessment: First-degree AV block with intermittent second-degree type I block. In a patient with myotonic dystrophy type 1 these represent conduction system disease of DM1.

Plan: No pacing indication at present. Annual ECG and ambulatory monitor, sooner for symptoms. He is to report any fainting, near-fainting or new breathlessness promptly. Anesthesia teams should be told of his DM1 and conduction disease before any procedure.

Meds: none. Allergies: NKDA.
cc: primary care

documents.title: Cardiology follow-up reviewed
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: April cards note finally in. Monitor: 1st degree AVB with intermittent 2nd degree type I, mostly asleep, longest pause 2.2 s, nothing higher grade. Added 2nd degree AVB type I. Annual ECG/monitor with cardiology. Monitor report itself was not included; not chasing further since the findings are in the note.

documents.title: Missed physical
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Called pt about yesterday's missed physical. He overslept after a late inventory shift. Rebooked Tues 11/18, 8:30.

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Annual, rescheduled from October. Feels about the same. Hands still slow to let go. Walking rather than jogging. No fainting. Neuromuscular follow-up is set for January.

Wt 75, down from 77.5 in January; he has not been trying to lose. Eating normally per pt.

Problems: DM1; first-degree AVB with intermittent 2nd-degree type I (cardiology following yearly); Klinefelter 47,XXY with azoospermia; s/p bilateral cataract surgery.
Meds: none. NKDA.

Exam: Lean. Frontal balding. Heart rate irregular at times, no murmur. Lungs clear. Slow grip release; mild ankle dorsiflexion weakness bilaterally.

A/P: Health maintenance. CBC, CMP, A1c, TSH. Flu shot today. Weight down 2.5 kg this year: recheck at next visit, ask neuro to weigh in. PHQ-2 1.

documents.title: Lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Your blood count, chemistry panel, thyroid and A1c from Tuesday are all normal. Mention the weight change at your neurology visit in January, and we'll check it again when I see you next.

reports.text: Sinus rhythm with prolonged PR interval. Normal QRS duration and morphology. No acute ST or T wave change.

documents.title: Neurology follow-up (visit 01/27/2026)
documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
NEUROMUSCULAR CLINIC: FOLLOW-UP
Date of service: 01/27/2026

Diagnoses: myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DMPK ~420 CTG repeats); Klinefelter syndrome 47,XXY; first-degree AV block with intermittent second-degree type I block (cardiology following); bilateral cataract extraction at 20.

Interval history: Handshakes are again hard to release. He notices his face is weaker, food is harder to get down, and he has lost weight without trying. He also reports less interest in sex than before.

Meds: none. Allergies: NKDA. Never smoker, no alcohol. Works part-time in retail.

Examination: Wasting of the temporalis and masseter muscles on both sides. Atrophy of the intrinsic muscles of the hands. Grip myotonia persists. Heart rhythm irregular on auscultation.

Laboratory (drawn today): CK 120 U/L (ref 38-174). Fasting glucose 90 mg/dL. Total testosterone 220 ng/dL, low. FSH 15 mIU/mL and LH 14 mIU/mL, both elevated.
ECG today: first-degree heart block.

Impression: Progression of DM1 with bulbar involvement (dysphagia) and weight loss. Primary testicular failure, as expected with Klinefelter syndrome, now with low testosterone and reduced libido.

Plan:
1. Modified barium swallow with speech-language pathology.
2. Continue yearly cardiology surveillance; irregular rhythm noted today.
3. Low testosterone to be addressed by primary care.
4. Return to clinic in 12 months.

cc: primary care

documents.title: Neurology letter reviewed
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Neuro f/u reviewed. Dysphagia, facial weakness, weight loss. T 220 with high FSH/LH, libido down. MBS ordered by them. Have staff move his visit up; will repeat AM testosterone here.

documents.title: Scheduling
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Per PCP, offered pt an earlier visit to go over the neurology results. Booked 3/3 at 8:00 so a morning blood draw can be done at the visit. Pt aware.

documents.title: Modified barium swallow study (02/24/2026)
documents.author: speech-language pathology
documents.body:
MODIFIED BARIUM SWALLOW STUDY
Date: 02/24/2026
Referred by: neuromuscular clinic, DM1 with dysphagia

Consistencies: thin and nectar-thick liquid by cup and straw, puree, soft solid, cracker.

Findings: Oral phase with mildly reduced bolus control. Swallow initiation delayed. Pharyngeal residue in the valleculae and pyriform sinuses after solids, cleared with a second swallow. No laryngeal penetration or aspiration with any consistency.

Impression: Mild oropharyngeal dysphagia.

Recommendations: Regular diet. Small bites, eat slowly, alternate solids with sips of liquid, use a second swallow as needed. Repeat study if symptoms progress.

Allergies: NKDA.

events.reason: Follow-up after neurology: swallowing, weight loss, low testosterone

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Here after his January neuromuscular visit and the swallow study. Food, meat and bread especially, feels like it hangs up and he has to swallow twice. No choking, no coughing with drinks, no pneumonia. Face feels weaker and friends say he looks thinner in the face. Has lost weight without trying. Eating three meals but slower. Sex drive lower than a year or two ago. Mood ok, PHQ-9 4.

O: Wt 72.5 (75 in Nov, 77.5 last Jan). BP/HR fine. Temporal and masseter hollowing. Thenar and interosseous wasting both hands, slow grip release. Heart irregular at times, no murmur. Lungs clear.

Swallow study 2/24: mild oropharyngeal dysphagia, residue clears with second swallow, no aspiration. Regular diet with strategies.

A/P
1. Oropharyngeal dysphagia, DM1. Follow SLP strategies; he has the handout. Call for choking, cough with meals or fevers.
2. Unintentional weight loss, about 5 kg in a year. Likely DM1 progression with slower eating. Calorie-dense snacks between meals. CBC, CMP, TSH, A1c today. Weigh at each visit.
3. Low testosterone (220 at neurology, high FSH/LH) with lower libido. Repeat morning testosterone drawn now, 08:30. Will discuss treatment and fertility at next visit.
4. DM1, conduction disease, Klinefelter: per specialists.
RTC 4 weeks.

documents.title: Testosterone and other labs
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Zachary, your morning testosterone came back at 228, low again and close to the neurology result. Blood count, chemistry, thyroid and A1c are normal. Before we talk about testosterone treatment we need to talk about whether you and your partner still want to try for a biological child, because testosterone can make that harder. We'll go over it on April 1.

documents.title: RE: Testosterone and other labs
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Yeah we still want to try at some point. We'll talk about it before the appointment. Thanks.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

orders.reason: Klinefelter syndrome, azoospermia, low testosterone; fertility options before testosterone therapy

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Follow-up. Swallowing about the same, using the second swallow and sips, no choking. Eating more snacks. Libido still low, no other complaints. He and his partner talked it over: they still hope to have a biological child at some point and want to know their options before he starts anything.

O: Wt 72.0 (72.5 in March). BP/HR normal. Facial and hand wasting as before. Heart irregular at times.

Labs: AM testosterone 228 (3/3), 220 with FSH 15 and LH 14 at neurology (1/27). CBC, CMP, TSH, A1c normal.

A/P
1. Male hypogonadism, primary (testicular), Klinefelter. Two low morning values with high gonadotropins. Testosterone would help libido, energy and bone, but it shuts down what little sperm production there may be. Agreed to see reproductive urology first about sperm retrieval options; no testosterone for now. Referral placed.
2. Weight loss, slowing. Continue extra calories. Recheck weight next visit.
3. Dysphagia: SLP strategies.
4. DM1 with conduction disease: cardiology yearly visit coming up in May.
Physical in the fall.
